h1: Pairing beer with nuts crisps and other bar snacks
title: Beer with Nuts, Crisps and Bar Snacks | Craft Beer School
desc: Simple pairings of beer with salted nuts, crisps, masala peanuts, bhujia and other bar snacks. Why salt, fat and bitterness work together.
teaser: Nobody orders a beer and a tasting menu at the same time. Most of us eat a handful of something salty. That is a pairing.
standfirst: Bar snacks do a job: they add salt, fat and crunch to a drink that cleans the palate. Choose the pair on purpose and both taste better. Here is a short guide for nuts, crisps and the Indian snacks that fill the bowl.
sections: Why snacks and beer suit each other

Salt makes you thirsty and makes the next sip taste fuller. Fat coats the tongue. Beer's carbonation and bitterness lift that coating off, so the next bite tastes fresh again. That is the whole engine of bar food. It is also why a bowl of peanuts empties so fast.

If you want the principles behind it, our guide on beer and food pairing basics explains three moves: match, contrast and cleanse. Snacks use mostly the last two.

Plain salted peanuts are the classic partner for a pale lager. The lager is light and crisp, so it refreshes between handfuls and does not fight the roasted flavour of the nut. Roasted cashews are creamier and sweeter. They suit a wheat beer or a gentle pale ale. Almonds with a dry roast and a little salt go well with a malty amber or a brown ale, because the toasted notes in the malt echo the nut.

Sweetened or candied nuts need a different beer. A rich, roasty stout or porter can take the sugar and the toast. A very bitter IPA will clash with sweetness and taste harsher.

Plain salted potato crisps are a gift to almost any beer, because the grease and salt need something fizzy. Hoppy pale ales cut through the oil well. Pilsners do too. Salt and vinegar crisps ask for something with sweetness, such as a wheat beer or a malty lager, to tame the sharpness.

Banana chips and tapioca chips, popular across Kerala and Tamil Nadu, are salty and a little sweet. A light lager or a fruity wheat beer works with them. Spicy chips need low bitterness, because chilli and bitterness amplify each other.

Indian bars have their own bowl. Masala peanuts are salty, spicy and crunchy. They suit a lager or a witbier with a little citrus. Bhujia and sev are fried gram flour, salty and sometimes hot. A pilsner or a pale lager cools the heat and cleans the oil. Roasted chana and namkeen mixes are drier and nuttier. A malt-forward amber ale suits them.

Our guide on Indian food and beer pairing goes further, with full dishes. For snacks, keep it simple: light beers for hot, oily snacks. Save the big IPAs for something that can take them.

A good home experiment costs very little. Pour small measures of three different beers, say a lager, a wheat beer and an amber ale. Taste each with no snack, then with a salted peanut, then with a piece of bhujia. Note how bitterness, sweetness and body change. Often the beer you liked least on its own is the one that improves most with food.
When to reach for something stronger

A strong, dark beer wants a richer snack. Dark chocolate covered almonds suit a stout. Smoked almonds suit a smoked beer or a porter. Salted cashews and a barley wine can be lovely, though the combination is rich enough to be a dessert.

You might also try cheese cubes with crackers. For more on that route, read beer and cheese pairing. Pairings are suggestions, not rules. If you like a combination, it works.
What a stale bowl does to beer

A bowl of nuts left on a bar for a day absorbs moisture and goes stale. Stale nuts taste of cardboard. That note makes any beer next to them taste off. Salted snacks also carry grease, which can spoil the head of a beer if it gets onto the glass rim. Bars that care about both change the bowl daily and wash glasses with no residue.

If you serve snacks at home, put out a small bowl and refill it. Do not leave a large one sitting for hours.

Salty snacks make people thirsty, which is not an invitation to drink faster. Put water on the table, pace yourself and never drive after drinking. Remember that nuts are a common allergen, so tell guests what is in the bowl and keep a nut-free option on the side. Offer a non-alcoholic beer or a soda as an alternative.

faqs: What snacks go best with lager?
Salted peanuts, plain crisps, masala peanuts and bhujia. A light, crisp lager cleans the palate between bites.
Can I serve nuts with a hoppy IPA?
Yes, but choose salted roasted nuts. Sweet nuts and very spicy nuts tend to make a hoppy beer taste harsher.
What beer goes with masala peanuts?
A lager or a witbier. Both are light enough to cool the spice and refresh the palate.
Should I worry about nut allergies at a tasting?
Yes. Tell guests what is in the snack bowl and keep a nut-free choice available.
